title: States of the Middle East, 2400 BCE–1886
summary: Among the smaller states of Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Arabia, Iran and the South Caucasus were Bronze and Iron Age kingdoms (Ebla, Mari, Yamhad, Kizzuwatna, Arzawa, Ugarit, Aram-Damascus, Ammon, Moab, Edom, Mannaea), the city-kingdoms of Cyprus, Characene, Elymais, Hatra, Kinda and Muhammad's state at Medina; the Caucasian kingdoms and emirates of the 9th–12th centuries (Tbilisi, Lori, Kakheti-Hereti, Syunik, Kars) and the dynasties of the 'Iranian intermezzo' (Sallarids, Rawwadids, Hasanwayhids, Kakuyids, Marwanids, Uqaylids, Mirdasids, Mazyadids, Ikhshidids); the Burids of Damascus, the Nizari Ismaili castles, the atabegs of Azerbaijan, Fars, Luristan and Kerman; the eastern Anatolian beyliks (Saltukids, Mengujekids, Shah-Armens, Artuqids, Eretnids, Kadi Burhan al-Din, Erzincan, Tacettin, Lâdik, Alaiye); the Mamluk pashas of Baghdad; Arabian states from the Sulayhids to the Jabrids, Bani Khalid, Kathiri, Mahra and Lahej; and the South Caucasus khanates of 1747–1828. Few pre-modern sources describe frontiers.
dataNote: Cliopatria's borders leave out many states of Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Arabia, Iran and the South Caucasus. This layer adds 76 of them. The South Caucasus khanates replace the border data's single 'Khanates of the Caucasus'. Dates and capitals come from cited reference articles; borders are reconstructions checked against Shepherd's Historical Atlas and the descriptions in those articles. Every line here is approximate.

regions.name: Ebla
regions.note: The first Eblaite kingdom of the archive period (Royal Palace G), the dominant power of north-western Syria until its destruction c. 2300 BCE, attributed to Sargon or Naram-Sin of Akkad. The archive names many dependent towns; the extent (Amuq to the Euphrates bend at Emar, south to Hama) follows the usual modern reading and is approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ebla'.

regions.name: Mari (Lim dynasty)
regions.note: The Amorite Lim dynasty of Mari controlled the middle Euphrates from Terqa to the Suhum border and the lower Khabur. Between the two periods of Lim rule Mari was held by Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia (his son Yasmah-Addu as king); Hammurabi of Babylon conquered Zimri-Lim in 1761 and destroyed the city c. 1759 BCE. Middle chronology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mari, Syria'.
regions.dataNote: Drawn as two slices, before and after Shamshi-Adad's rule.

regions.name: Yamhad
regions.note: Amorite kingdom centred on Halab (Aleppo), the leading Syrian power of the 18th century BCE (Yarim-Lim I and Hammurabi I had some twenty vassal kings). The core realm ran from the Amuq to the Euphrates bend and south to the Qatna frontier. Ended by the Hittite conquests of Hattusili I and Mursili I (Aleppo destroyed c. 1600/1595 BCE). Middle chronology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Yamhad'.
regions.dataNote: Only the core realm is drawn, from the Amuq to the Euphrates bend and south to the Qatna frontier; vassals such as Alalakh lie inside.

regions.name: Kizzuwatna
regions.note: Kingdom of the Cilician plain and the Anti-Taurus up to Kummanni (Comana), independent between the Hittite Old and New Kingdoms and alternately allied to Hatti and Mitanni; absorbed by the Hittites in the early 14th century BCE. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kizzuwatna'.

regions.name: Arzawa
regions.note: Arzawa Minor, the chief state of the Arzawa lands of western Anatolia, with its capital at Apasa (Ephesus); its king Tarhundaradu corresponded with Amenhotep III. Mursili II conquered it c. 1320 BCE and divided it into the vassal kingdoms of Mira, Hapalla and the Seha River Land. It stretched roughly from the Hermus to the Maeander and inland to the Lakes. Sources: Wikipedia 'Arzawa'.
regions.dataNote: The extent (Hermus to the Maeander, inland to the Lakes) is approximate.

regions.name: Ugarit
regions.note: Coastal kingdom of Ras Shamra between Mount Casius (Jebel Aqra) and the Siyannu border, a vassal first of Egypt and from c. 1350 BCE of the Hittites, but ruled by its own dynasty until its destruction c. 1185 BCE. Area about 2,000 km². Sources: Wikipedia 'Ugarit'.
regions.dataNote: The inland border is approximate.

regions.name: Bit Adini
regions.note: Aramaean kingdom on both banks of the Euphrates below Carchemish, with its capital at Til Barsip (Tell Ahmar); Shalmaneser III of Assyria took it from Ahuni in 856 BCE and renamed the capital Kar-Shalmaneser. Sources: Wikipedia 'Bit Adini'.
regions.dataNote: Carchemish (drawn by the border data among the Neo-Hittite states) is left outside.

regions.name: Aram-Damascus
regions.note: Aramaean kingdom of Damascus and the Hauran. Under Hazael (c. 842–796 BCE) it dominated Israel and took Gilead and Bashan. Tiglath-Pileser III annexed it in 732 BCE. Sources: Wikipedia 'Aram-Damascus'; Shepherd plate 5 (750–625 BCE).
regions.dataNote: The middle slice extends to the Jabbok.

regions.name: Ammon
regions.note: Kingdom east of the Jordan between the Jabbok and the Arnon around Rabbath Ammon (Amman); an Assyrian tributary from 734 BCE, absorbed after the Babylonian campaign of 582 BCE. The frontier with Moab moved repeatedly. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ammon'.
regions.dataNote: The line here is a compromise.

regions.name: Moab
regions.note: Kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon/Madaba plains and the Zered (Wadi Hasa); King Mesha's stele (c. 840 BCE) records its revolt from Israel and expansion north of the Arnon. An Assyrian tributary from 734 BCE; conquered by Nebuchadnezzar II in 582 BCE. Start date approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Moab'.

regions.name: Edom
regions.note: Kingdom south of the Zered as far as the Gulf of Aqaba, with its capital at Bozrah (Busayra); it broke from Judah in the mid-9th century BCE, paid tribute to Assyria from 734, and fell to Nabonidus of Babylon c. 552 BCE. The western border on the Arabah is approximate; Edom later expanded into the Negev. Sources: Wikipedia 'Edom'; Shepherd plate 5.
regions.dataNote: Later Edomite expansion into the Negev is not drawn.

regions.name: Mannaea
regions.note: Kingdom south and south-east of Lake Urmia (capital probably Izirtu, near Saqqez), a buffer between Urartu and Assyria; absorbed by the Medes after 616 BCE. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mannaea'.
regions.dataNote: Extent approximate.

regions.name: Marion
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria (until 609), Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. No ancient source gives the kingdoms' frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ancient history of Cyprus' and the city's article; Shepherd plate 5.
regions.dataNote: The island-wide division into kingdoms is a modern reconstruction from the location of the capitals, sanctuaries and the main valleys; every line is conjectural. Start date simplified to 600 BCE (after the end of Assyrian domination in 609).

regions.name: Paphos
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria (until 609), Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. Nicocles of Paphos survived the 312 BCE abolition until 306 BCE.

regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria (until 609), Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. Sold to Kition in the 340s BCE, then given to Salamis by Alexander (332 BCE).

Kition (Phoenician dynasty) annexed Idalion c. 450 BCE and bought Tamassos in the 340s; Alexander gave Tamassos to Pnytagoras of Salamis (332 BCE).

regions.name: Salamis
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. No ancient source gives the frontiers between the kingdoms. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ancient history of Cyprus' and the city's article; Shepherd plate 5. The leading kingdom; Evagoras I briefly united most of the island (c. 391–380 BCE). Tamassos (332–312 BCE) was Alexander's gift to Salamis.
regions.dataNote: The island-wide division into kingdoms is a modern reconstruction from the location of the capitals, sanctuaries and the main valleys; every line is conjectural. regions.name: Characene
regions.note: Kingdom at the head of the Persian Gulf founded by Hyspaosines after the Seleucid collapse; capital Charax Spasinou. Frequently a Parthian vassal but with its own kings and coinage until Ardashir I annexed it c. 222. Sources: Wikipedia 'Characene'.
regions.dataNote: Drawn over the Parthian outline.

regions.name: Elymais
regions.capital: Seleucia on the Hedyphon; Susa at times
regions.note: Autonomous kingdom in the Zagros foothills of Khuzestan (Susiana), often a Parthian vassal; held Susa at times. Conquered by Ardashir I c. 221. Sources: Wikipedia 'Elymais'.
regions.dataNote: Extent approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Araba (Hatra)
regions.note: Arab kingdom of the caravan city of Hatra in the Jazira steppe, under Parthian suzerainty; its rulers took the title 'king of the Arabs' from the mid-2nd century. It repelled Trajan (117) and Septimius Severus (198/199) and fell to the Sasanian Shapur I in 240/241. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hatra' and 'Kingdom of Hatra'.
regions.dataNote: Only the steppe around the city is drawn.

regions.name: Kindah Kingdom
regions.note: Hujrid kings of Kinda ruled the Ma'add tribes of north and central Arabia c. 450–550, as clients of Himyar; their power collapsed after al-Harith ibn Amr's death in 528. Their tribal hegemony (Najd and al-Yamama) had no fixed frontier. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kinda'.
regions.dataNote: The area drawn (Najd and al-Yamama) is a rough indication of tribal hegemony, not a frontier.

regions.name: First Islamic state (Medina)
regions.note: The polity Muhammad founded at Medina in 622 under the Constitution of Medina. It held the Medina oasis (622–627) and grew after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya and the conquest of Khaybar (628–629); after the conquest of Mecca (630), Hunayn and Ta'if it held most of the Hejaz, Tihama and western Najd (630–632). The many deputations of 630–631 brought looser allegiances from the rest of Arabia. Succeeded by the Rashidun Caliphate. Sources: Wikipedia 'First Islamic state' and 'Constitution of Medina'.
regions.dataNote: Slices: the Medina oasis (622–627); after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya and the conquest of Khaybar (628–629); after the conquest of Mecca (630), Hunayn and Ta'if, most of the Hejaz, Tihama and western Najd (630–632). The looser allegiances of 630–631 from the rest of Arabia are not drawn. The Rashidun Caliphate is drawn by the border data from 633.

regions.name: Emirate of Tbilisi
regions.note: Arab emirate based in Tbilisi from 736; effectively independent of the caliphate from the 830s (Ishaq ibn Ismail, crushed by Bugha al-Kabir in 853), later a city-state ruled by its emirs and then a council of elders until David IV of Georgia took it in 1122. At first it held central Kartli, later only the city's district. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Tbilisi'.
regions.dataNote: The first slice covers central Kartli, the second only the city's district.

regions.name: Emirate of Tbilisi
regions.note: Arab emirate based in Tbilisi from 736; effectively independent of the caliphate from the 830s (Ishaq ibn Ismail, crushed by Bugha al-Kabir in 853), later a city-state ruled by its emirs and then a council of elders until David IV of Georgia took it in 1122. At first it held central Kartli, later only the city's district. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Tbilisi'.
regions.dataNote: The first slice covers central Kartli, the second only the city's district.

regions.name: Kingdom of Lori (Tashir-Dzoraget)
regions.note: Kiurikian (Bagratid) kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget in northern Armenia, nominally a vassal of Ani; the Seljuks took Lori in 1065 and the dynasty survived in Tavush and Matsnaberd until the 12th century. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget'.
regions.dataNote: The Tavush and Matsnaberd remnant (to the 12th century) is not drawn.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti
regions.note: Georgian kingdom of Kakheti and Hereti, independent of the united Kingdom of Georgia from c. 1014 until David IV annexed it in 1104. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti'.
regions.dataNote: The border data folds it into Georgia; drawn on top.

regions.name: Kingdom of Syunik
regions.note: Armenian kingdom of Syunik (Kapan), 987–1170. In 1104 the Seljuks took Kapan; afterwards it was reduced to a few fortresses (Baghaberd) until 1170. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Syunik'.
regions.dataNote: Drawn to 1104. Its frontier on the Aras and with Nakhchivan is approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Vanand (Kars)
regions.note: Bagratid kingdom of Kars (Vanand), founded 963 by Mushegh, brother of Ashot III of Ani; its independence from Ani is uncertain. Ceded to Byzantium by Gagik-Abas in 1065. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Vanand'.

regions.name: Shaddadids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of Dvin and Ganja ruling Arran (between the Kura and the Karabakh hills) from Ganja until the Seljuk takeover of 1075. A junior branch then governed Ani for the Seljuks and Georgians to 1199. Sources: Wikipedia 'Shaddadids'.
regions.dataNote: Drawn at Ganja until 1075. The junior branch at Ani (to 1199) is not drawn, a vassal.

regions.name: Sallarid dynasty
regions.note: Daylamite dynasty (Musafirids) that took Azerbaijan in 941 under Marzuban ibn Muhammad; ruling Azerbaijan until the Rawwadids replaced them in the 980s. Their hold on Arran and Armenia was looser. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sallarid dynasty'.
regions.dataNote: Drawn over Azerbaijan until the 980s. Their hold on Arran and Armenia is not drawn.

regions.name: Rawadid dynasty
regions.note: Kurdicised Arab dynasty of Tabriz that ruled Azerbaijan in the late 10th and 11th centuries; Wahsudan submitted to Tughril in 1054 and the Seljuks ended the line in 1071. Sources: Wikipedia 'Rawwadid dynasty'.

regions.name: Hasanwayhids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of the western Jibal (Dinavar, Kermanshah, Hulwan, Shahrizur), recognised by the Buyids; collapsed by 1015 and replaced by the Annazids. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hasanwayhids'.

regions.name: Kakuyids
regions.note: Daylamite dynasty related to the Buyids that ruled Isfahan and Hamadan from c. 1008 (Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar, Avicenna's patron) until Tughril took Isfahan in 1051; afterwards they were Seljuk atabegs of Yazd (to 1141). They briefly held Rayy. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kakuyids'.
regions.dataNote: The Yazd atabegate (to 1141) is not drawn. Their brief hold on Rayy is not drawn.

regions.name: Marwanids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of Diyar Bakr centred on Mayyafariqin (Silvan) and Amid, holding Ahlat and Manzikert for much of the period; ended by the Seljuks in 1085. Sources: Wikipedia 'Marwanid dynasty (Diyar Bakr)'.
regions.dataNote: The border data shows this area as Byzantine; drawn on top.

regions.name: Uqaylid dynasty
regions.note: Arab dynasty of Mosul controlling the Jazira (Nisibis, Sinjar, at times Harran and Raqqa); its height under Muslim ibn Quraysh (1061–1085), who briefly held Aleppo. Mosul passed to the Seljuks in 1096. Sources: Wikipedia 'Uqaylid dynasty'.
regions.dataNote: Extent approximate.

regions.name: Mirdasid dynasty
regions.note: Arab dynasty of the Banu Kilab ruling the emirate of Aleppo, more or less continuously from Salih ibn Mirdas's capture of the city in 1024 (earlier claims from 1014) until 1080. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mirdasid dynasty'.

regions.name: Mazyadid dynasty (Banu Mazyad)
regions.note: Arab Banu Asad dynasty ruling an autonomous emirate between Kufa and Hit, from c. 961 under the Buyids and then the Seljuks; al-Hilla, founded as their camp, became the capital. Sadaqa I (1086–1108) was the strongest ruler; the emirate ended c. 1150–1160. Sources: Wikipedia 'Banu Mazyad'.
regions.dataNote: Extent approximate.

regions.name: Burid dynasty (Emirate of Damascus)
regions.note: Turkic dynasty founded by the atabeg Toghtekin, ruling the emirate of Damascus (with the Hauran, Baalbek and at times Homs) nominally under the Seljuks; Nur ad-Din took Damascus in 1154. Sources: Wikipedia 'Burid dynasty'.
regions.dataNote: Extent follows Shepherd's plate 'Asia Minor and the States of the Crusaders in Syria, about 1140' (Emirate of Damascus).

regions.name: Ikhshidid dynasty
regions.note: Turkic governors of Egypt for the Abbasids, in practice autonomous: Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid held Egypt and Palestine from 935 and, after the 944–947 settlement with the Hamdanids, southern Syria with Damascus; the Fatimids took Fustat in 969. They also held nominal suzerainty over the Hejaz. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ikhshidid dynasty'.

regions.name: Nizari Ismaili state (Rudbar)
regions.note: The Alamut state founded by Hasan-i Sabbah in 1090: a network of castles rather than a contiguous realm. It held the Rudbar valley of Alamut, Quhistan (from 1091), Girdkuh (from 1096) and the Jabal Bahra castles in Syria (acquired from the 1130s; Masyaf 1140/41). The Mongols took Alamut in 1256; Girdkuh held out to 1270 and the Syrian castles fell to Baybars by 1273. Sources: Wikipedia 'Nizari Ismaili state'.

regions.note: Iranian dynasty of Tabaristan (Mazandaran), 651–1349, alternating between independence and vassalage; among its lines were the Ispahbadiyya (1074–1210) and the Kinkhwariyya (1238–1349). Sources: Wikipedia 'Bavand dynasty'.

regions.note: Turkmen atabegs of Fars, vassals first of the Seljuks and then of the Khwarazmshahs and the Mongols, but ruling Fars as a hereditary state until the reign of Abish Khatun, married to an Ilkhanid prince, in the 1280s. Sources: Wikipedia 'Salghurids'.

regions.name: Hazaraspids
regions.note: Kurdish (Fadluyid) atabegs of Greater Lur in the Zagros, from the mid-12th century until the Timurids ended them in 1424. Wikipedia dates the dynasty from 1115; 1155 is the usual date for Abu Tahir's atabegate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hazaraspids'.
regions.dataNote: Extent approximate.

regions.name: Qutlugh-Khanids
regions.note: Khitan dynasty of Kerman founded by Buraq Hajib, vassals of the Mongols; ended 1306/07. Sources: Wikipedia 'Qutlugh-Khanids'.

regions.name: Eldiguzids (Atabegs of Azerbaijan)
regions.note: Atabegs of Azerbaijan, founded by Shams al-Din Eldiguz (atabeg from 1136), who controlled the Seljuk sultans of Iraq and with them Azerbaijan, Arran and the Jibal (1146–1194); after Tughril III's death (1194) they held Azerbaijan and Arran until Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah took Tabriz in 1225. Sources: Wikipedia 'Eldiguzids'.

regions.note: Turkmen beylik of Erzurum founded after Manzikert (1071). Annexed by the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in 1202. Sources: Wikipedia 'Saltukids'.

regions.name: Mengujekids
regions.note: Turkmen beylik of Erzincan, Kemah, Şebinkarahisar and Divriği; the Erzincan line was annexed by Rum in 1228 (the Divriği branch lasted to 1277 as a vassal). Sources: Wikipedia 'House of Mengüjek'.

regions.name: Ahlatshahs (Shah-Armens)
regions.note: The Shah-Armens of Ahlat on Lake Van (Bitlis, Van, parts of Muş), 1100–1207; Ahlat passed to the Ayyubids in 1207. Sources: Wikipedia 'Shah-Armens'.

regions.name: Artuqids
regions.note: Turkmen dynasty with branches at Hasankeyf (from 1102; at Amid from 1183), Mardin (from 1106/08) and Harput (1112–1234). Amid was held by the Inalids until 1183 and by the Artuqids from 1184 to 1231; after the Ayyubids took Hasankeyf and Amid (1232) only the Mardin branch remained, a vassal of the Mongols and Turkmen confederations until the Qara Qoyunlu ended it in 1409. Sources: Wikipedia 'Artuqids'.

regions.name: Eretnids
regions.note: Founded by Eretna, the Ilkhanid governor of Anatolia, who declared himself sultan after the Battle of Karanbük (1343); his realm covered central and eastern Anatolia (Sivas, Kayseri, Amasya, Erzincan, Erzurum). After his death (1352) the east fell away (Erzincan became autonomous) and the state was reduced to the Sivas–Kayseri core; Kadi Burhan al-Din took over in 1381. Sources: Wikipedia 'Eretnid dynasty'.

regions.name: Kadi Burhan al-Din's state
regions.note: Kadi Burhan al-Din, the Eretnid vizier, took over the Eretnid lands in 1381 and ruled them as sultan from Sivas until he was killed by the Aq Qoyunlu c. 1398; Bayezid I then annexed Sivas. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kadi Burhan al-Din'.

regions.name: Beylik of Erzincan (Emirate of Erzincan)
regions.note: Emirate centred on Erzincan, autonomous after Eretna's death (1352) under Ahi Ayna and his successors; Mutahharten (1379–1403) was a vassal of Timur. Annexed by the Qara Qoyunlu c. 1410. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Erzincan'.

regions.name: Beylik of Tacettin
regions.note: Small Turkmen principality of Niksar and the coast at Ünye and Çarşamba (the Byzantine Limnia), 1348–1428, wedged between Trebizond, the Eretnids and the Ottomans. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Limnia'.

regions.name: Beylik of Lâdik (İnançoğulları)
regions.note: The İnançoğulları beylik of Lâdik (Denizli), from the Seljuk collapse of the 1260s; later dependent on the Germiyanids and absorbed c. 1368. Sources: Wikipedia 'Beylik of Lâdik'.
regions.dataNote: The border data shows the area as Hamid and Germiyan territory; drawn on top. Dates from Wikidata (Q717451).

regions.name: Beylik of Alaiye
regions.note: Alanya (Alaiye) and its hinterland, semi-autonomous after the Seljuk defeat at Köse Dağ (1243) and a beylik from c. 1293, at times under the Karamanids or Lusignan Cyprus; briefly passed to the Mamluks in the 1420s and was taken by the Ottomans in 1471. Sources: Wikipedia 'Alaiye'.

regions.name: Mamluk dynasty of Iraq
regions.note: The Georgian mamluk pashas of Baghdad, from Hasan Pasha (1704) and his son Ahmad to Dawud Pasha, governed Baghdad and Basra (with Shahrizor at times) with near-complete autonomy from the Ottoman sultan until the Ottoman reconquest of 1831. Mosul was under the Jalilis. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mamluk dynasty of Iraq'.

regions.name: Sulayhid dynasty
regions.note: Ismaili dynasty founded by Ali al-Sulayhi in 1047, allied to the Fatimids; at its height (1063–1067) it ruled most of Yemen. It held the northern highlands (1047–1055) and later the central highlands from Sana'a to Dhu Jibla (1066–1138, under Queen Arwa from 1084). Sources: Wikipedia 'Sulayhid dynasty'.

regions.name: Bani Khalid Emirate

regions.name: Kathiri Sultanate
regions.note: The Kathiri sultanate (established 1379) ruled most of Hadhramaut; its strongest period was under Badr Bu Tuwayriq (1516–1565) and his successors, when it held the Wadi Hadhramaut and the coast at al-Shihr and Mukalla. The Zaydi imamate occupied Hadhramaut from 1658; in the 18th–19th centuries the state was fragmented. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kathiri'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Lahej

Covered c. 19,500 km² (central Armenia, Iğdır, Sharur); taken by Russia in October 1827 and ceded at Turkmenchay (1828). Sources: Wikipedia 'Erivan Khanate'.
